title: worker_threads: Isolate Separation vs MessagePort Communication
prerequisites: Understanding of threads and shared memory

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A bakery has one main shop and several separate prep kitchens. Each prep kitchen has its own oven, its own pantry (its own storage), and its own staff — but they're all part of the same building (same process). Kitchens talk by sending finished goods through a dumbwaiter — messages are copied, so a cake sent is a copy, not the same cake. But they can also agree on a shared ingredient shelf that everyone can reach — the same shelf, same contents, visible to all kitchens at once.
progressiveExplaining.junior: worker_threads let you run JavaScript in parallel on separate threads: const worker = new Worker('./worker.js'); worker.postMessage(data); worker.on('message', ...). Each worker has its own V8 isolate (own JS heap, own event loop), so they run truly in parallel on multi-core machines — unlike the single main thread. Communication is via postMessage (structured clone, copying) or Transferable (ArrayBuffer/MessagePort, zero-copy by detaching). For shared memory: SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics let threads read/write the same bytes safely. Use workers for CPU-bound work (parsing, hashing, image processing) that would block the main thread.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, each worker_thread is a separate V8 isolate with its own heap and event loop, sharing the process (and its OS resources). This gives true parallelism for CPU-bound JS — the main thread can't be parallelized, but workers can. Communication: postMessage uses structured clone (copy) by default; transferring an ArrayBuffer detaches it from the sender and hands the same backing store to the receiver (zero-copy). MessagePort is the underlying channel (workers have a parent port). SharedArrayBuffer provides shared memory with Atomics for synchronization. The trade-offs: memory overhead per isolate, and shared state requires discipline (Atomics or message passing).
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Each worker_thread is backed by a V8 Isolate and its own libuv loop/thread (or reuses a loop in the process for I/O). The parent creates a MessagePort pair; postMessage serializes the value (structured clone via V8 serializer, or transfers via detaching ArrayBuffer/moving MessagePort), and the receiver deserializes in its isolate. A SharedArrayBuffer is a single OS memory region mapped into both isolates' address spaces — writes are visible across threads; Atomics.* operations compile to atomic instructions (lock-prefixed on x86, LDXR/STXR on ARM) providing synchronization. The worker's lifetime is managed by the Worker object; terminate() can forcibly stop it. The pool of workers is application-managed (Node doesn't auto-pool them).

codeComparison.title: CPU work on the main thread vs offloaded to a worker
codeComparison.summary: Heavy CPU work blocks the event loop; a worker thread runs it in parallel and communicates via postMessage.

legacyOrBad.label: CPU-bound work on the main thread
legacyOrBad.snippet: const result = expensiveParse(hugeData); // ❌ OLD: blocks the event loop

modernOrGood.label: Worker thread offload
modernOrGood.snippet:
const worker = new Worker('./parse-worker.js'); // ✅ NEW: parallel thread
worker.postMessage(hugeData); // ✅ NEW: copy via structured clone

interviewGotchas.question: How is a worker_thread different from a child_process, and when would you choose each?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the parallelism taxonomy — interviewers want the isolate-in-process vs separate-process distinction and the use cases (CPU-bound JS vs isolation/crash protection).
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: A worker_thread is a separate V8 isolate inside the SAME process: it shares the process's memory space, file descriptors, and can use SharedArrayBuffer for zero-copy shared memory. It's the right tool for parallelizing CPU-bound JavaScript (parsing, crypto, image ops) while keeping the process single and communication cheap. A child_process is a completely separate OS process: its own memory space, its own V8 instance, communication only via IPC (serialized messages) — heavier to spawn, but it provides crash isolation (a child crash doesn't take down the parent), the ability to run non-JS binaries, and separate resource limits. Choose worker_threads for JS parallelism with shared memory; child_process for isolation, external programs, or when you want the OS to manage the boundary.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'workers are just lighter processes'. They share the process and can share memory (SharedArrayBuffer), which changes the correctness model (races) — processes can't corrupt each other. Another trap: assuming worker_threads make the main thread faster — they parallelize OFF the main thread; the main thread's own work is unchanged. Candidates who describe the isolate-vs-process boundary show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between postMessage copying, transferring, and SharedArrayBuffer, and when do you use each?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the communication mechanisms — interviewers want the structured-clone copy, the zero-copy transfer (detach), and the shared-memory option with its synchronization requirement.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: postMessage(value) by default STRUCTURE-CLONES the value: the receiver gets a deep copy in its own isolate — safe, but O(n) time and memory for large buffers. Transferring (postMessage(buffer, [buffer])) DETACHES the ArrayBuffer from the sender and hands the same backing store to the receiver — zero-copy O(1), but the sender loses access (byteLength becomes 0). SharedArrayBuffer creates a single shared memory region both threads can access concurrently — no copy at all, but writes are visible across threads and require Atomics for synchronization (or you get data races). Use: clone for small/config messages, transfer for one-way large buffers where the sender is done, SAB for genuinely shared state that both threads read/write concurrently (with Atomics).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'transfer and SAB are the same'. Transfer moves ownership (sender loses it); SAB shares ownership (both can use it anytime). Another trap: using SAB without Atomics for coordination — shared memory without synchronization is a data race, and Node can't detect it. Candidates who distinguish copy/transfer/share show real concurrency understanding.
